newsitem.title: UK: Payrolls data could cloud U.S. bond outlook.
newsitem.headline: Payrolls data could cloud U.S. bond outlook.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries will tackle most of this week's run of American data with ease, outperforming European bond markets on signs of slowing economic growth, market analysts forecast on Monday.
But they said the bullish tone could do an about-face on Friday if the crucial but volatile U.S. payrolls statistics prove to be the Achilles' heel of Treasuries yet again.

The raft of data, which includes the employment cost index on Tuesday, third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) on Wednesday and October payrolls on Friday, will determine whether the Federal Reserve needs to act on interest rates in the fourth quarter, economists said.

"If we get a reasonably good employment cost index and GDP data and home sales, there is scope for the market to move higher. Spreads will narrow against other markets," said Adam Chester at Yamaichi International.

According to a Reuters poll, economists expect the U.S. employment cost index, a measure of wage inflation and important indicator of future inflationary pressures, to rise 0.8 percent in the third quarter, unchanged from the second-quarter rate.
Third quarter GDP on Wednesday is seen rising 1.9 percent, a significant slowdown from the 4.7 percent growth in the second quarter and showing more evidence that U.S. growth is cooling.

Chester, an international bond strategist, said the data could prompt the 10-year Treasury/German Bund spread to narrow to 55 basis points (0.55 percentage point) by Friday, ahead of the U.S. jobs data, from its current 64 basis points.
"We recommend moving to a neutral or short position (in Treasuries) going into Friday's payrolls number because all the good news ends there," he said.
Non-farm payrolls data are a key element in determining labour market tightness and are closely watched by markets for signs of future inflationary pressures.
Economists expect payrolls to rise by 239,000 in October after September's surprise 40,000 drop. U.S. unemployment is expected to be steady at 5.2 percent of the workforce.
Daiwa economist Katy Peters agreed the payrolls number on Friday might spook investors into a sell-off.
"Our feeling is that most of the week the Treasury market will remain range-bound in the 110-112 range," said Peters. December T-bonds are currently around 111.

"But we think non-farm payrolls will be larger than the market expects, at around 250,000...and on balance the report will be negative for Treasuries. It will call for some reassessment of the outlook for interest rates."
This reassessment will prompt Treasuries to underperform German Bunds in the weeks ahead, Peters added. "Ten-year spreads could push up to around 70 within a week and a half," she said.
ABN AMRO Hoare Govett economist Brian Venables agreed that Treasuries had upside potential this week.
"The U.S. definitely has more potential to go up. Spreads could narrow," he said. "We're looking to a 10-year Bund spread in the mid 50s if the data go well."
He said payrolls were the wild card and could upset the market. "But we have to assume that the economy has been slowing down and payrolls can only confirm that."

Other data this week includes consumer confidence on Tuesday, home sales and the Federal Reserve's Beige Book on Wednesday, personal income and weekly jobless claims on Thursday and the National Association of Purchasing Management index on Friday.

After all that, obstacles in the weeks ahead will put a lid on gains in Treasuries, with U.S. elections on November 5 and a Federal Open Market Committee meeting on November 13 keeping investors sidelined, economists said.
Both Venables and Chester were unenthusiastic about the performance of Treasuries in the longer term.

"We're coming into a crucial period for the U.S. economy with the key Christmas retail sales period ahead," said Chester, adding this could push economic growth up to around 3.0 percent in the fourth quarter. "In the long term we're more negative on inflation."

Venables agreed growth was unlikely to be as weak as expected between now and the end of the year. This, coupled with steady Bunds, meant the spread had the potential to widen out to around 90 basis points by the first quarter of 1997, he added.
